messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Re: Changing data column from text to decimal
parts:
Sorry Philip, there's no labour saving way to do this I'm afraid. I suggest you
delete the offending columns, then add them again as decimal, then re-import
your data. The whole process will hopefully only take a few minutes (depending
on how much data you have, as the import can be slow for very big datasets).

Why can't it change the type? This is because the distance data file is actually
a database (Microsoft Access format), and you can't change the type of a field
in a database. I could have written code that gets around this by allowing you
to choose a new type, then add a temporary field of the new type, convert and
copy the data, delete the old field, rename the new field (you can rename).
However, I was worried that the type conversion would not go smoothly, and it
seemed such an obscure feature I didn't get around to it. If you think it would
be useful then please go to the Distance web site, click on "report a bug" and
use the Bugzilla site to request it as a feature.

Cheers - Len

--

messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Re: Changing data column from text to decimal
parts:
> > DistData mdb and change the field type without needing to re-import
> > everything? My very large dataset is a drag to keep re-importing.

Yes, you can do this, if you have an ancient version of Access, or your version
will allow you to upgrade the database but then export it afterwards back into
Microsoft Access 2.0 format. The "native" version of Access to use is Access
97. Note that it is not sufficient to change the field type; you also have to
change the entry in the DataFields table corresponding with that field -- change
the FieldType from 3 (i.e., Text) to either 2 (Decimal) or 1 (Integer). The
format of the DistaData.mdb is documented in a help appendix "Inside Distance".

I didn't mention this before as it's black-belt stuff. But you're clearly a ninja.

> > 2. Why is
> > the DistData mdb created in an ancient version of Microsoft Access that makes
> > it impossible to edit using queries and such if you only have Access 2007 or
> > newer? Is it so that clumsy tinkerers like me don't screw it up?

Not at all. It's because Distance is ancient! When I wrote the database
interface, this stuff was cutting edge! Since then Microsoft have completely
changed the way you can program database stuff twice -- this is not something we
have the resources to keep up with I'm afraid.

Cheers - Len
